angle: machine and physics limits — Shapeoko 5 Pro / 5.1 Pro w/ VFD spindle kit
note_on_method: Every number below is tagged type: 'cited' (with source_url, quoted/paraphrased from a primary Carbide3D or third-party page) or 'derived' (shows the formula and inputs used). Several Carbide3D spec pages do not publish the number a rigid industrial router chart would assume (max feed/rapid, torque curve) — those gaps are stated explicitly rather than filled with guesses.

machine_specs.spindle_used_in_calcs: 80mm water-cooled VFD spindle kit (2.2kW) — Carbide3D states this is the VFD kit sold for 5 Pro / 5.1 Pro

spindle_torque_vs_rpm_curve.note: Carbide3D's own 80mm spindle doc page does not give a power/torque curve, torque at low RPM, or a stated base/rated frequency. Confirmed absent on https://carbide3d.com/hub/docs/80mm-spindle-kit (fetched directly). This means we cannot cite how much power/torque is actually available at 16-18k RPM vs the rated 2.2kW — only general VFD-motor physics (below).

vfd_power_derating_general_physics.statement: Induction-motor VFD spindles are typically constant-torque below a base (rated) frequency and constant-power above it; available power falls roughly linearly with RPM below base speed. This is standard AC induction motor/VFD behavior, not a number specific to this spindle (Carbide3D does not publish the base frequency for the 80mm unit). Because 16-18k RPM sits in the upper half of this spindle's 8-24k range, it is more likely to be near full rated power than the low end (8-10k RPM) would be — but this is an inference from general VFD behavior, not a verified curve for this part.

collet_and_max_cutter.value: ER-20 collet, 1/8in / 1/4in / 1/2in sizes included; max cutter shank 1/2in (12mm)

motion_system.value: Ballscrew-driven on all axes (not belt). X/Y ballscrew: 16mm diameter, 20mm pitch, with wiper. Z ballscrew: 16mm diameter, 10mm pitch (1610), carried over from the Shapeoko HDM to lift the heavier 80mm spindle. Linear rails: HG-15. No belts, no round/unsupported rails, no leadscrews or gear racks.

ballscrew_accuracy.value: +/- 50 micrometers per 300mm (ballscrew lead accuracy spec, not a measured whole-machine positioning accuracy)

step_resolution.value: X/Y step length 0.012mm, Z step length 0.006mm

gantry_rigidity_spec.note: Carbide3D does not publish a gantry/frame deflection or stiffness number anywhere in the fetched spec/shop pages. This is a real unquantified limit beyond the single-tool deflection calculated below — the whole gantry, not just the 1/4in cutter, can flex under cutting load, and that is not bounded by any number in this file.

max_feed_and_rapid_rate.type: gap on Carbide3D's own spec page — filled with community/forum reports only, clearly flagged
max_feed_and_rapid_rate.carbide3d_official_spec_page_status: https://carbide3d.com/shapeoko5pro-specs/ lists no max feed or max rapid rate at all.

community_reports.claim: Shapeoko 5 Pro ships configured to 200 IPM (5080 mm/min) XY and 100 IPM (2540 mm/min) Z by default; GRBL/firmware ceiling is ~275 IPM (6985 mm/min) if settings are changed, limited by step-pulse generation rate of the controller.
A user reports running (older, pre-5) Shapeoko Pro machines at 400 IPM (~10,000 mm/min) in soft plastic, stating that is the factory GRBL ceiling for that machine.
community_reports.type: cited (forum, different/older machine model — 'Shapeoko Pro' not '5 Pro' — included for context only, not applied to the 5 Pro)

max_feed_and_rapid_rate.relevance_to_this_analysis: Both candidate feed rates computed below (about 64 IPM and about 108 IPM, see calcs.mrr_and_power) are well under even the conservative 200 IPM factory default. The machine's feed/rapid ceiling is not the binding constraint for the birch-ply full-slotting case in this file.

mrr_and_power.purpose: Material removal rate and spindle power needed, 1/4in (6.35mm) 2-flute cutter, full slot (width of cut = cutter diameter) in birch plywood, at two bounding candidate settings.
formula: Vf (feed rate, mm/min) = RPM x fz (chipload, mm/tooth) x z (flute count)
MRR (mm3/min) = Vf x D (cutter diameter, mm) x DOC (depth of cut, mm)   [full slot: radial width = D]
P (W) = MRR (mm3/min) x Ke (specific cutting energy, J/mm3) / 60

cited_but_not_used_directly.context: 15mm birch (Betula pendula) plywood, drilling dowel/eccentric-joint/confirmat holes, 8mm drill, 6000 RPM, 2 m/min feed. Values are whole-machine 'specific cutting work' (measured from total energy draw) per mm3 of hole volume.
cited_but_not_used_directly.why_not_used_for_this_calc: Plugging this directly into the MRR formula above gives absurd results (>100kW for a 3mm-deep slot pass), which is a red flag, not a real spindle-power requirement. The likely reason: drilling a small hole removes very little volume while the spindle motor, acceleration, and fixed machine overhead energy stay roughly constant, so dividing total energy by a tiny removed volume massively inflates J/mm3 relative to the energy actually spent shearing wood. This number measures a different thing (whole-system energy per small drilled hole) than the per-volume shear energy an MRR-based spindle-power estimate needs. Reported here for transparency, not used below.

derived_estimate_used.derivation: Standard machining 'unit power' framework (Up, hp per in3/min of MRR) used for spindle-sizing in shop/machining handbooks: P(hp) = MRR(in3/min) x Up. Converting Up to J/mm3: Ke[J/mm3] = Up[hp/in3/min] x 745.7 W/hp / (16387 mm3/in3 / 60 s/min) = Up x 2.73. Mild steel Up is roughly 1.0 hp/in3/min, aluminum alloys roughly 0.2-0.3 hp/in3/min (both commonly cited round numbers in machining-handbook unit-power tables, not individually re-verified here). Wood is softer and shears far more easily than aluminum, so its Up — and thus Ke — should sit below aluminum's. 0.15-0.6 J/mm3 is used as a bounding estimate on that basis (equivalent to roughly 0.05-0.22 hp/in3/min).
derived_estimate_used.caveat: This is an order-of-magnitude engineering estimate, not a number read off a primary source for wood specifically. Treat the resulting power numbers as 'almost certainly well under 2.2kW' rather than as a precise prediction.

mrr_and_power.comparison_to_spindle: Even at the high-estimate end of the derived Ke band (0.6 J/mm3) and the most aggressive candidate setting (18k RPM / 0.003in / 9mm DOC), estimated cutting power is about 1.57 kW against a 2.2kW rated spindle (about 71% of rated power). At the conservative setting (16k RPM / 0.002in / 3mm DOC) it is about 0.08-0.31 kW (4-14% of rated power). Spindle power is not the limiting factor across this whole candidate grid under this estimate; it only gets tight (>1.5kW) at full 9mm depth combined with the highest chipload and highest Ke estimate simultaneously.

tool_deflection.purpose: Cantilever deflection of the 1/4in (6.35mm) solid carbide cutter at 25mm stickout, under the tangential cutting force implied by the power estimates above.
formula: I (mm4) = pi x d^4 / 64   (second moment of area, round shaft)
v (m/s) = pi x D x RPM / 60000   (cutter OD surface speed)
Ft (N) = P (W) / v (m/s)   (tangential cutting force from power and surface speed)
delta (mm) = Ft x L^3 / (3 x E x I)   (cantilever beam tip deflection, point load at tip, fixed base)

carbide_modulus_E.note: Range reflects cobalt-binder content (grade HCA ~635 GPa at 5.5% Co, grade H-91 ~575 GPa at 11% Co); 600 GPa used as the mid-range reference value per this source.

fixed_inputs.caveat: Ft used here is tangential force only; true resultant (tangential + radial) force on a milling cutter is somewhat higher — commonly 1.1-1.3x tangential in wood cutting — so these deflections are a lower-bound estimate, not a worst case.

tool_deflection.interpretation: All derived deflections are under 0.015mm (15 microns) even in the aggressive 9mm-deep scenario, because a 1/4in solid carbide shank at only 25mm stickout is very stiff (deflection scales with L^3, so short stickout dominates). At these force levels, tool deflection is not the binding limit either — the bottleneck for full-slotting birch ply on this machine is more likely chip evacuation, heat, and the unquantified gantry rigidity (see machine_specs.gantry_rigidity_spec gap) than either spindle power or single-tool bending.

min_chipload_rubbing_burning.purpose: Lower bound on chipload to avoid rubbing/burning in wood.

critical_chip_thickness.type: cited (secondary/industry guide, not an independently verified primary engineering source)
critical_chip_thickness.statement: Critical chip thickness for clean cutting of hardwood is cited as approximately 0.05mm; below this the tool rubs rather than shears, generating friction heat that burns the surface.
critical_chip_thickness.caveat: This number came back aggregated across several CNC-router feeds/speeds guide pages in search results (toolgrit.com and cncwoodguide.com both surfaced similar figures); the exact original attribution could not be independently re-verified by direct fetch within this task's tool-call budget. Treat as industry-guide-sourced, not textbook/peer-reviewed-sourced.

typical_minimum_chipload_ranges_for_6mm_.type: cited (same caveat as above — aggregated from CNC router feeds/speeds guides)

min_chipload_rubbing_burning.comparison_to_candidate_settings: Candidate chiploads 0.002-0.003in = 0.0508-0.0762mm sit right at or just above the cited ~0.05mm critical chip thickness floor, and below the low end of the cited 0.08-0.20mm 'typical' hardwood/plywood range. This means the 0.002in end of the candidate range is marginal — close enough to the rubbing/burning threshold that it should be treated as a floor, not a comfortable working point, especially if the actual spindle RPM runs above the nominal setpoint (RPM accuracy on this VFD spindle is only specified to +/-5%, per the 65mm spindle kit page, which raises actual chipload-at-the-edge uncertainty).

rpm_accuracy_caveat.note: Cited from the 65mm VFD spindle kit announcement; Carbide3D does not separately publish an RPM-accuracy figure for the 80mm unit on its own doc page, so this is carried over as the best available same-family number, flagged as such.

recommended_envelope.chipload_range_in: 0.0025-0.003in (avoid the bottom of the 0.002in end — it sits at/near the cited ~0.05mm rubbing/burning floor)
recommended_envelope.max_doc_mm_full_slot: 6mm per pass for routine production; 9mm is power- and deflection-feasible per the derived estimates above (about 0.3-1.6kW and under 15 microns tool deflection) but pushes chip load per the toolgrit-sourced ranges and removes nearly 2.5x the chips per pass of a 3mm-deep pass, so chip evacuation/heat — not spindle power or tool stiffness — is the real risk at 9mm on a dust-boot-and-vacuum hobby/school setup.
recommended_envelope.rationale: Spindle power (2.2kW cited) and single-tool deflection (<15 microns at 25mm stickout, 600GPa carbide, cited) both have wide margin across the full candidate grid per the derived estimates in this file, even acknowledging those estimates are order-of-magnitude (Ke band) rather than measured. The real constraints this machine imposes that a rigid industrial-router feeds/speeds chart would not show are: (1) no published torque curve for the VFD spindle below its rated band, so low-RPM cuts (<10-12k RPM) should not be assumed to have full rated power, even though 16-18k RPM is clear of that concern; (2) no published gantry/frame stiffness number, so whole-machine deflection beyond the single tool is a real but unquantified risk at the higher end of the depth range; (3) the machine's own feed/rapid ceiling (200-275 IPM, forum-sourced) is not binding at these chiploads — do not let that drive settings down further than the chipload floor requires.
